Dear Dr. Harrison,

Thank you for seeing Leo Jenkins, a five-year-old boy referred for a specialist opinion. He lives with his parents and attends full-time kindergarten.

Leo’s history dates back to 8 months of age, when he experienced a brief convulsion provoked by a high fever. More recently, his parents have described recurrent, lightning-fast muscle jerks affecting his upper limbs, primarily in the mornings. Crucially, they report no bilateral whole-body convulsive episodes, sustained stiffening postures, or sudden loss of postural tone resulting in drop attacks. There are no staring spells with behavioral arrest, nor has he exhibited localized motor twitching, isolated focal events with preserved awareness, or episodes marked by impaired responsiveness.

Developmentally, Leo has met all his milestones appropriately, with no comprehensive delays across early domains and no cognitive impairment or learning deficits. Physical and neurological examinations today were entirely normal, with intact cranial nerves, symmetrical motor strength, and normal coordination.

A recent routine electroencephalogram demonstrated distinct epileptiform disturbances featuring generalized paroxysmal spike-wave activity. Neuroimaging was unremarkable; specifically, the MRI showed no widespread cerebral parenchymal volume loss, attenuation of the callosal body, or underdevelopment of the cerebellar midline structures. White matter volume was fully preserved without diminution, central nervous system myelination was mature with no lags, and there was no evidence of mesial temporal or hippocampal scarring.

He is taking no medications, and the family history is unremarkable for neurological conditions. I would greatly appreciate your evaluation and thoughts on an appropriate management strategy.

Sincerely,

Dr. Eleanor Vance
